name: NPS Enhanced
license: Not clearly Apache/MIT-permissive per repo — repo shows a LICENSE file (original NPS project used MIT/AGPL variants historically; this fork's LICENSE file was not read in full text, treat as unverified — GitHub badge area did not show an explicit SPDX license tag on the summary page)
language: Go (server, client, web UI in Go + JS frontend)
popularity: ~1.1k GitHub stars, 154 forks, 11 watchers, 1,937 commits — a very active fork ('enhanced/二开') of the original ehang-io/nps project (which itself had much larger adoption in the Chinese self-hosting community). Has spin-off sub-projects: Android client (npsclient), OpenWrt build, and a mirror repo.
maturity: Actively maintained fork with continuous commits and automated Release CI (GitHub Actions 'Release' workflow badge present), regular binary releases for Linux/Windows/Android/OpenWrt. No red flags — this is one of the more actively developed projects in the batch.
client_requirements: Client (npc) is a single static Go binary installed via a shell/PowerShell installer (install.sh/install.ps1) or manual download; runs as a background service (npc install/start/stop) without requiring a TAP/TUN virtual network interface for basic TCP/HTTP/UDP/SOCKS5 tunneling. Client install script uses 'sudo sh' for the Linux installer (to register as a system service), so root/admin is used for the convenience install, though the binary itself could likely be run directly without root for simple foreground TCP/HTTP proxying. Not a fully admin-free workflow out of the box.
server_requirements: Full server source available (Go), self-hostable single binary (nps) with a bundled Web UI for configuration and client/tunnel management. Config-file plus Web UI driven; the Web UI does have backend HTTP endpoints (used internally by its own JS frontend) but there is no documented public/stable REST API or TypeScript/JS SDK intended for third-party programmatic tunnel registration — it's designed to be operated via its own web console, not integrated into an external control plane.
server_language: Go (backend), JS (bundled web admin UI, not a public SDK)
has_programmable_api: false (or unconfirmed) — the Web UI likely calls internal HTTP endpoints, but no documented/stable public REST API or client library for third-party programmatic tunnel registration was found in the README.
viability_notes: Solid, actively maintained, self-hosted Go tunnel server with single-binary client and server, but the client install path defaults to sudo/service-registration and there's no documented external API for our SvelteKit app to hit — we'd have to reverse-engineer its internal web UI endpoints or shell out to CLI/config files. Reasonable fallback if we're willing to drive it via config files/CLI rather than a clean API.

name: reverst
popularity: ~1.0k GitHub stars, 46 forks, 4 watchers, 105 commits. Backed by Flipt (a known feature-flag company), used as their tunnel component; moderate but respectable open-source adoption.
maturity: Actively maintained by Flipt-io; has CI (Dagger-based unit/integration tests), docs, examples, and a management-address flag, suggesting ongoing development. No obvious abandonment signals.
client_requirements: Client is a Go library (go.flipt.io/reverst/client) built on net/http std-lib abstractions — no TAP/TUN, no admin/root needed; it's a Go server-side library that dials out and registers with the tunnel group, not a foreign network interface. However, this means integrating requires embedding it into a Go program (there's also a CLI 'reverst' client binary via `go install ./cmd/...`) — using it from a non-Go local client means running the compiled CLI binary, which appears to be lightweight, no elevated privileges required.
server_requirements: Full server source available (Go). Server (reverstd) is config-driven via a tunnel-groups YAML file (local file or k8s ConfigMap) for defining tunnel groups/auth; there IS a `--management-address` flag exposing an HTTP 'management API' for the server, though the README doesn't fully detail its exposed operations (likely limited to introspection rather than full tunnel CRUD). No JS/TypeScript SDK — Go-only client library.
has_programmable_api: Partial — Go client library (true, language=Go, used to register tunnel groups programmatically from Go code) but no JS/TypeScript server SDK; there is a `--management-address` HTTP management API on the server whose scope isn't fully documented in the README (appears more for ops/introspection than tunnel registration, which is config-file driven via tunnel-groups YAML).
viability_notes: Clean Go design (QUIC/HTTP3, load-balanced tunnel groups, permissive Apache-2.0 license) with an admin-free lightweight client binary, which is attractive for a hosted server binary. However it's Go-native (no TS/JS server API) and tunnel-group registration is YAML/config-file driven rather than a full HTTP control plane for dynamic per-tenant tunnel registration, so our SvelteKit app would need to shell out to config file writes or use the limited management API.

name: PageKite
language: Python (pure Python 2/legacy-oriented implementation; project began in ~2010 era)
popularity: 751 GitHub stars, 122 forks, 38 watchers, 1,492 commits — pagekite.net itself is a long-standing (since 2010) commercial+open-source tunneling service with historically wide adoption (early ngrok-alternative, popular in Raspberry Pi/DIY hosting communities), though the codebase's era shows.
maturity: README explicitly states 'This program is under active development and the contents of this repository may at times be somewhat unstable' but also 'For stable releases... see pagekite.net/downloads'. Commit history is long but the project's design/tech (targets Python, historically Python 2) is dated. Red flag: pure Python implementation from the early-2010s era, unclear modern Python 3 packaging or contemporary maintenance cadence — treat as legacy/slow-moving rather than abandoned.
client_requirements: PageKite's `pagekite.py` is a pure Python script/CLI — no TAP/TUN interface needed, no root/admin required for typical use (just a Python interpreter, e.g. `python pagekite.py 80 mysite.pagekite.me`). Special install note: needs a Python 2/3 runtime present (project historically Python2-first; check current main branch's Python version compat before relying on it) — this is a soft complexity cost compared to a single static binary, but no elevated privileges.
server_requirements: Front-end (server) source is available in the same PyPagekite repo (the 'remote front-end protocol' implementation) — self-hostable, but it is config/CLI-driven (flags/config file, no REST/HTTP control-plane for programmatic registration). No TypeScript/JavaScript SDK; there's a legacy 'jsui' directory for a UI but not a management API.
has_programmable_api: false — no documented REST API or JS/TS SDK for programmatic tunnel registration; operation is via CLI flags/config files.
viability_notes: Client is admin-free and TUN-free (a real plus), but requires a Python runtime, and the project is a legacy pure-Python codebase with no modern control-plane API — we'd need to shell out to CLI/config files for every tunnel, and the AGPL-3.0 license is more restrictive for a hosted-server product. Workable as a fallback but not a strong fit.

name: rustunnel
popularity: 656 GitHub stars, 48 forks, 3 watchers, 315 commits. Has a hosted managed service (rustunnel.com) with pay-as-you-go pricing, plus MCP-server integration for AI agents (Cursor/Claude Code/Windsurf) and a Skillselion listing — indicates decent traction, and it's positioned directly as an 'ngrok alternative.'
maturity: Actively developed: CI badge, recent AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md/MCP integrations, dashboard UI, roadmap doc, contribution guidelines with pre-push hooks. No abandonment red flags; looks like a currently-maintained, evolving project (possibly relatively new but fast-moving).
client_requirements: Client is a single Rust binary (`rustunnel`) with a setup wizard (`rustunnel setup`), CLI flags (`rustunnel http 3000`), and a `--json` machine-readable output mode. No TAP/TUN network interface — it's a WebSocket-based reverse tunnel client, no admin/root required for typical CLI usage (only production *server* deployment docs mention systemd/root, not the client).
server_requirements: Full server source available (Rust) — self-hostable, OR use their hosted edge servers (eu/us/ap regions) directly, meaning we could adopt the hosted server without running our own if desired, but the ask is to self-host it. Server exposes a documented REST API (dashboard port, default 8443) with Bearer-token auth: GET/DELETE /api/tunnels, GET /api/tunnels/:id/requests, POST/DELETE /api/tokens, GET /api/history, plus a machine-readable OpenAPI 3.0 spec at /api/openapi.json. Note: the REST API is for tunnel introspection/management/token issuance/history — actual tunnel *creation* still happens by the client dialing the control-plane WebSocket (port 4040) with a token, not via a 'create tunnel' REST call.
has_programmable_api: true — language=Rust backend exposing REST/OpenAPI (HTTP+JSON) for listing/closing tunnels, managing API tokens, and viewing captured request history/replay; dashboard frontend is TypeScript. Tunnel *registration* itself is still client-initiated via WebSocket handshake with a pre-issued token (which itself IS creatable via POST /api/tokens), so a control-plane-driven workflow (mint token via REST, then start rustunnel client with token) is achievable.
viability_notes: Best-fit client story in the batch: single Rust binary, no TAP/TUN, no root required, plus a genuine documented REST/OpenAPI control-plane (with a TypeScript dashboard) we could integrate with our SvelteKit app to mint tokens and monitor/manage tunnels programmatically. Main caveats: AGPL-3.0 license (copyleft implications for a hosted product) and tunnel creation itself is still client-CLI-driven rather than a pure 'create tunnel via POST' API — we'd combine REST token-issuance with client launch.

name: onionpipe
language: Go (with CGO/libtor bindings for the static-binary build option)
popularity: 617 GitHub stars, 37 forks, 9 watchers, 157 commits — moderate niche popularity within the Tor/privacy tooling community.
maturity: Automated releases on every commit to main (Docker image publishing), Renovate bot configured for dependency updates — actively maintained infra, but the feature set is narrow/single-purpose (Tor-based forwarding) and a 'control plane for SDN orchestration' is only a stated future idea, not implemented.
client_requirements: DISQUALIFYING: onionpipe requires and bundles a Tor daemon (`tor` binary in $PATH, or a statically-linked libtor for the standalone build requiring openssl/libevent/zlib C library dependencies to build). Every tunnel setup spins up a real Tor circuit, adding substantial latency/overhead and installation complexity (Tor daemon dependency, or a heavy CGO build with native library deps) — this directly conflicts with the 'no complex install' constraint, independent of TAP/TUN or root concerns (no TAP/TUN or root is required, but Tor daemon + circuit overhead is a hard architectural cost).
server_requirements: No traditional 'server' component in the reverse-tunnel-provider sense — the 'server' is the Tor network itself (onion services); there is no self-hostable control-plane server binary to deploy, and no REST/JS API for registering tunnels programmatically beyond the onionpipe CLI/config.
server_language: N/A (relies on the Tor network, not a custom server)
has_programmable_api: false — CLI-only tool; no REST/JS API; a YAML config mode and a possible future 'control plane for SDN orchestration' are only roadmap ideas, not implemented.
viability_notes: Disqualified: fundamentally Tor-dependent (bundles/requires a Tor daemon and pays real onion-circuit latency/overhead), has no conventional self-hosted server or API, and doesn't fit a hosted-server-binary + lightweight-client architecture at all. Not worth deeper research beyond confirming this mismatch.

name: Port Buddy
language: Java (CLI client compiled to GraalVM native image; server/gateway/net-proxy in Java/Spring Boot; web dashboard in TypeScript/React)
popularity: 535 GitHub stars, 48 forks, 2 watchers, 195 commits. Has a companion community-built GUI project (portbuddy-gui) and its own hosted service (portbuddy.dev) — a fairly polished, ngrok-alternative-styled project.
maturity: Active-looking multi-module project with GitHub Actions CI, Docker images per service, and a full microservices architecture (cli/server/gateway/net-proxy/eureka/ssl-service/web) — suggests real engineering investment, though it's more complex/heavier infrastructure than a single small binary+server pair.
client_requirements: CLI client (`portbuddy`) is described as a GraalVM-native command-line application (Java 25), i.e., compiles to a native binary — no TAP/TUN interface, and usage examples (`portbuddy 3000`) don't indicate any admin/root requirement for basic use; can also run the CLI via Docker. Reasonably simple, single-binary-style installation via the native image, though the underlying stack (Java 25 + GraalVM) is heavier to build from source than most competitors (prebuilt binaries would be needed to keep this simple for our client).
server_requirements: Full server source available. Architecture is a multi-service Spring Boot backend: `server` (Tunnel Management API), `gateway` (WebFlux API Gateway), `net-proxy` (TCP/UDP proxy), `eureka` (service discovery), `ssl-service` (automated TLS), and a React+TypeScript `web` dashboard. The server module is explicitly described as an 'API & Tunnel Management' service (Spring Boot), implying an HTTP/REST control-plane exists for tunnel management, though the README doesn't show explicit REST endpoint docs/examples for third-party programmatic registration — would need to inspect the `server` module source directly to confirm exact API surface.
server_language: Java (Spring Boot backend), TypeScript/React (web dashboard, not a management SDK for external apps)
has_programmable_api: Likely true (unconfirmed in README) — language=Java/Spring Boot 'server' module explicitly billed as '(API & Tunnel Management)', suggesting a REST API for tunnel lifecycle exists; would need source-level verification to confirm request/response shapes and whether it supports external client tunnel registration vs. purely CLI-registered tunnels.
viability_notes: Client is a native-image single binary (admin-free, TUN-free) and the server explicitly has an 'API & Tunnel Management' Spring Boot module, which is promising for programmatic control — but the overall system is a heavier multi-service microservices architecture (Eureka discovery, separate gateway, ssl-service) versus a simple single-binary server, raising self-hosting operational complexity, and the true REST API surface for external registration is unverified from the README alone.

name: tunnl.gg
popularity: 547 GitHub stars, 44 forks, 6 watchers, but only 23 commits total — small, young, single-purpose project (its own hosted instance is at tunnl.gg).
maturity: Small commit count (23) suggests a young/lean project rather than a long-maintained one; no explicit red flags of abandonment, but limited history makes long-term maintenance unproven. Purpose-built and minimal by design ('minimal SSH tunneling service').
client_requirements: No custom client binary at all — the 'client' is just the standard OpenSSH client (`ssh -t -R 80:localhost:8080 proxy.tunnl.gg`). This is about as admin-free/TUN-free/simple as it gets (no install beyond having ssh, which is virtually always preinstalled), though it does mean the local machine needs outbound SSH access and there's no fine-grained programmatic client SDK — it's literally an ssh reverse port-forward.
server_requirements: Full server source available (Go, ~6MB static binary). Server is entirely config-driven via environment variables (SSH_ADDR, HTTP_ADDR, HTTPS_ADDR, STATS_ADDR, DOMAIN, TLS cert paths, etc.) and requires DNS wildcard + TLS certs (Let's Encrypt) for subdomain routing. There is a built-in stats/metrics endpoint but no documented REST/JS control-plane for programmatic tunnel registration — tunnels are ephemeral and created purely by the act of an SSH client connecting; there's no 'register a tunnel' API to call from our SvelteKit app, and no persistent/named-tunnel management via API.
has_programmable_api: false — no REST/JS API; server is env-var/config-driven, and tunnel creation is solely triggered by inbound SSH connections (ephemeral, auto-generated subdomains), not by any API call we could drive from a control plane.
viability_notes: The client-side story is arguably the simplest possible (plain ssh, no binary to distribute at all), but there's zero programmatic control plane — we cannot register/manage tunnels via HTTP from our app, only by shelling out an SSH command per tunnel, and tunnels are ephemeral/random-subdomain by design (no static naming without further engineering). Young project with limited commit history is an added maturity risk.

name: tunneller
maturity: DISQUALIFYING RED FLAG: repository was archived by the owner on Sep 10, 2025 ('It is now read-only') — the project is no longer maintained/accepting changes. Author's own README also explicitly warns their public hosted endpoint 'SHOULD NOT' be relied upon and 'is not secure.'
client_requirements: Client is a Go binary (`tunneller client -expose localhost:8080`) — no TAP/TUN interface and no admin/root apparently required for basic use, install via `go install` or downloading a release binary. Architecturally reasonable, but moot given the archived status.
server_requirements: Server source available (Go), but requires standing up and securing a separate Mosquitto MQTT message-bus (the client connects to an MQ topic, and the server publishes 'fetch this URL' commands over MQTT) — an unusual and more complex self-hosting dependency (an MQTT broker) versus a single self-contained binary. No REST/JS control-plane API for tunnel registration; entirely config/CLI + MQTT-topic driven, and author flags security concerns (malicious actors could inject fake requests via the message bus).
server_language: Go (server) + relies on external Mosquitto MQTT broker infrastructure
has_programmable_api: false — no REST/JS API; operates via CLI and an MQTT message bus.
viability_notes: Disqualified: the repository is archived/read-only as of Sept 2025 (no future maintenance possible), and even ignoring that, the architecture requires operating a separate MQTT broker with acknowledged security weaknesses and offers no programmatic HTTP API. Not worth further research.
